title: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscarawas County, OH
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Tuscarawas County, OH
metaDescription: Own oil and gas mineral rights in Tuscarawas County, Ohio? Learn how the Utica flank play, county records, and the Dormant Mineral Act shape your options.
heroLead: Tuscarawas County sits on the western flank of the Utica/Point Pleasant play, a wide agricultural county where mineral ownership is almost always a family inheritance question before it is a geology question.
intro: Tuscarawas County stretches across east-central Ohio, led by New Philadelphia as the county seat and dotted with smaller communities like Sugarcreek, Strasburg, Dover, Zoar, and Uhrichsville. Geologically, the county sits on the flank of the Utica/Point Pleasant fairway, west of the deep core counties of Harrison, Guernsey, and Belmont, which means pay thickness and initial production rates here have generally run lower than in the core, though permitted and producing wells exist across several townships.

For most families we talk with in Tuscarawas County, the mineral interest in question was reserved when a farm sold decades ago, then passed down through a will, sometimes several times, until what remains today is a fractional share split among cousins who may not even know each other. Understanding what you actually hold, and what it is realistically worth, starts with the same two things everywhere in the county: the deed records at the courthouse in New Philadelphia, and the current activity data the state maintains for your specific township.

sections.heading: The county's geology in plain terms
paragraphs: The Utica/Point Pleasant formation runs beneath most of eastern Ohio, but its thickness and richness in liquids vary considerably from county to county. Tuscarawas County is generally categorized as flank acreage, meaning the pay zone here tends to be thinner and the gas drier than in core counties immediately to the southeast.

That does not mean the county lacks activity. Operators have permitted and drilled horizontal wells in multiple Tuscarawas County townships over the past decade, particularly in areas closer to the county's eastern and southern edges where the formation improves. Whether a specific parcel has seen that activity depends entirely on its location, which is why we check township-level Ohio Department of Natural Resources data before ever discussing value with an owner.

sections.heading: How ownership typically breaks down here
paragraphs: Much of Tuscarawas County's farmland has been in continuous family ownership for generations, particularly in areas with significant Amish and Mennonite populations around Sugarcreek and Baltic. Where land has never been sold outside the family, mineral rights typically remain intact and unsevered.

In other parts of the county, especially around towns like Strasburg, Roswell, and Stone Creek, farms changed hands more frequently through the 1900s, and it is common to find a severed mineral interest, reserved by a prior owner and passed down independently of whoever farms the surface today. Both patterns exist side by side, and only a title search at the Tuscarawas County Recorder's office in New Philadelphia can confirm which situation applies to your specific tract.

It is also common for a single original mineral interest to now be split among a dozen or more heirs, each holding a small fraction after several generations of inheritance. Small fractional interests are not a problem; they are simply the norm across much of rural Tuscarawas County, and each co-owner can typically sell their own share independently of what other family members choose to do.

sections.heading: The Dormant Mineral Act in a flank county
paragraphs: Because so many Tuscarawas County mineral interests were reserved decades before shale drilling made them relevant, Ohio's Dormant Mineral Act, ORC 5301.56, comes up regularly here, particularly for surface owners trying to clear title on land where the mineral history is unclear. Under the current statute, a severed interest can be deemed abandoned after 20 years of no qualifying use, but only if the surface owner completes the required notice process and the mineral owner does not respond with a claim to preserve or evidence of use within 60 days.

The Ohio Supreme Court's 2016 decision in Corban v. Chesapeake Exploration confirmed that this notice-and-lapse process, not automatic reversion under the older 1989 law, is what actually governs. If you are a mineral owner in Tuscarawas County and have never leased, received a royalty, or filed anything on record, it is worth confirming your interest has not already been the subject of a notice before assuming you can sell it freely. We check the recorder's records for any DMA filings as a standard part of our title review.

sections.heading: Selling in Tuscarawas County
paragraphs: Whether your interest is producing, leased and unleased, or entirely undeveloped, the process starts with confirming ownership through the county recorder's records, then checking current activity for your specific township. From there we put together a written, no-obligation offer that reflects your documented percentage and the actual conditions on the ground, using hedged ranges tied to nearby activity rather than a flat promise.

Owners across the county, from Sugarcreek to Zoar to Uhrichsville, come to this decision from different starting points, some hold small inherited fractions, others hold producing interests with years of royalty history, and a few are untangling a title issue tied to an old deed or a dormancy question. We walk through your specific situation before quoting anything, and there is no pressure to accept an offer you are not comfortable with.

faqs.question: Is Tuscarawas County part of the Utica core or the flank?
faqs.answer: Tuscarawas County is generally considered flank territory, with thinner pay than core counties like Guernsey or Harrison, though activity exists in several townships closer to the county's eastern and southern edges.

faqs.question: My family has held the same farm in Tuscarawas County for generations. Do we own the minerals?
faqs.answer: Likely yes, since minerals typically stay attached to land that has never been sold, but this should be confirmed with a title search rather than assumed.

faqs.question: What if my mineral interest was reserved decades ago and never used since?
faqs.answer: It may be subject to a Dormant Mineral Act claim if a surface owner completes the required notice process, but abandonment is not automatic. We check recorded documents for any filings before quoting.

faqs.question: I only own a small fractional share inherited from a Tuscarawas County farm. Can I sell it?
faqs.answer: Yes. Small fractional interests, split among several heirs, are common across the county, and you can typically sell your own share independently of other co-owners.

faqs.question: How do I find out which township my mineral interest is in?
faqs.answer: The legal description on your deed identifies the section and township. We can help interpret it if you are unsure, especially for older deeds with unfamiliar formatting.
